Power Grid Corporation of India Limited

14. The Review Petitioner has contended that the Commission had disallowed the
time overrun of 85 days, i.e., time over-run of 59 days from 30.9.2022 to 28.11.2022
(delay due to transportation of 80 MVAR Bus reactor from Lucknow) and time over-
run of 26 days from 11.1.2023 to 6.2.2023 (time taken for Application to CEA for
Energisation to commissioning of the Subject Asset) in the impugned order and
consequently disallowed the IDC and IEDC of ₹43.33 lakh on account of delay not
condoned in the impugned order.
15. The Review Petitioner has further contended that the Commission did not
consider the MoM of the 11th CMETS dated 30.9.2022, wherein the earlier approved
125 MVAR Bus Reactor was modified to 80 MVAR Bus Reactor in view of the
transportation constraint and wherein it was recorded that the installation of the bus
reactor could take two to three months. The Commission ought to have condoned the
time overrun of 26 days for the period from 11.1.2023 to 6.2.2023 as the time was
availed by the CEA for inspection and carrying out the necessary requirements for
issuing the Energisation Certificate and the Review Petitioner had no control over the
internal processes or timelines of the CEA. Therefore, the Review Petitioner had no
control over the delay caused by the CEA. The Review Petitioner has also contended
that the Commission had erred in disallowing the IDC & IEDC on account of delay not
condoned and the events of the delay were beyond the control of the Petitioner.
Order in Review Petition No. 20/RP/2025 Page 12 of 22

20. We have considered the submission of the Review Petitioner. As per the
chronology of events submitted by the Review Petitioner, it is observed that the
Review Petitioner has claimed the time overrun on the basis of delay in issuance of
the Minutes of Meeting of the 11th CMETS held on 30.9.2022 (13 days), time lapsed
in arranging internal approvals for award of contract for transportation (24 days), for
issuance of bidding documents & subsequent LoA to the contractual agency M/S
Kataria Carriers (10 days) and time taken by the contractual agency for
commencement of transportation (12 days).
21. With regard to the time overrun of 13 days claimed by the Review Petitioner on
account of delay in issuance of Minutes of Meeting (MoM) of the 11th CMETS held on
30.9.2022, it is noted that the Review Petitioner was a participant in the said meeting
and, being a participant, was well aware of the discussions held in the meeting. it
recorded in the said meeting that the Review Petitioner should make efforts to
commission the asset by December 2022, in view of envisaged high voltage issues in
the upcoming winter season. Therefore, we are of the view that the Review Petitioner
ought to have proactively taken the necessary steps to transport the 80 MVAR Bus
Reactor from Lucknow to Chamera Substation early, without waiting for the issuance
of the Minutes of the Meeting of the aforesaid meeting on 13.10.2022. Accordingly,
the 13-day delay due to the issuance of the MoM does not justify the delay in
transporting the 80 MVAR Bus Reactor. Accordingly, the review on this count is
rejected.

items.subject: Petition under Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Article 10 of Power Purchase Agreement dated 18.12.2013 (Procurers PPA) and Schedule I (VIII) of the Power Purchase Agreement dated 19.12.2013 (PTC PPA) seeking compensation/consequential reliefs on account of occurrence of Change in Law event impacting revenues and costs during operating period. Adhunik Power and Natural Resources Limited
items.pdf_digest:
categorically, and unequivocally rejected the Petitioner’s Change in Law claim.
Both PTC and TNPDCL returned the supplementary invoices raised by the
Petitioner not merely on the ground that no prior determination of the
Commission had been obtained, but fundamentally because no Change in Law
entitlement was ever admitted under the contractual framework; no Change in
Law event was ever recognised or accepted by the Respondents; and the
mandatory contractual preconditions under Articles 10.3.3 and 10.3.4 requiring
prior determination of occurrence of the event as well as quantification of impact
by the Appropriate Commission were never fulfilled. Accordingly, the
Petitioner’s contention that the Respondents “did not dispute the occurrence of
the event” is wholly fallacious and erroneous.
(k) The Respondents’ insistence on prior adjudication by this Commission,
as contemplated under Articles 10.3.3 and 10.3.4 of the PPA, cannot be
mischaracterised as an admission of liability or acceptance of the Petitioner’s
claims. This requirement is a mandatory contractual condition precedent, and
the Respondents’ adherence to the same merely reflects compliance with the
PPA mechanism. It does not imply that the Respondents accept either the
occurrence of a Change in Law event or the Petitioner’s entitlement to any
compensation thereunder. In light of the above, the Petitioner’s allegation that
the Respondents did not dispute the occurrence of the alleged Change in Law
event is wholly misconceived, factually untenable, and legally unsustainable.
The said allegation is therefore liable to be rejected in limine.
(l) This Commission, vide Order dated 29.1.2020, dismissed Petition No.
305/MP/2015 filed by the Petitioner in relation to its PPA with WBSEDCL,
holding categorically that the cancellation of the Ganeshpur coal block does not
constitute a Change in Law event. The Petitioner thereafter preferred an
Appeal, and the APTEL, vide Order dated 4.9.2025, set aside the said decision
and remanded the matter. It is pertinent that TNPDCL was not a party to those
proceedings, nor was the TNPDCL PPA ever under consideration before either
this Commission or the APTEL in that context. It is relevant to note that in the
rejoinder filed by the Petitioner in Petition No. 305/MP/2015, the Petitioner
expressly stated, in response to the reply filed by TNPDCL, that TNPDCL had
been impleaded only for the limited purpose of demonstrating the composite
scheme, and that no relief whatsoever was being claimed under the TNPDCL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Order in Petition No. 845/MP/2025 Page 21 of 81

PPA. The Petitioner is misleadingly relying on APTEL’s judgment dated
4.9.2025 rendered exclusively in the context of the WBSEDCL PPA to persuade
this Commission to issue directions of a computational nature in the present
matter. The directions emanating from the APTEL judgment are inextricably
linked to the adjudication of rights and obligations under the WBSEDCL PPA.
Those directions arise solely in the proceedings remanded to this Commission
in respect of that PPA. The APTEL judgment does not concern TNPDCL, does
not adjudicate upon the TNPDCL PPA, and does not create any substantive or
procedural rights in favour of the Petitioner under the TNPDCL contractual
framework.
(m) The Petitioner’s claim is fundamentally predicated on the Orders dated
20.4.2023 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the cases of GMR Warora
and MSEDCL v. Adani Power. The Petitioner has expressly relied upon these
judgments as the basis for filing the present Petition. However, even assuming,
without admitting, that these judgments confer any benefit on similarly placed
parties, the Petitioner cannot take advantage of them, having failed to assert or
prosecute its rights diligently and at the appropriate time. The law is well settled
that the mere fact that relief has been granted to another similarly placed party
does not entitle a person who has slept over his rights to seek identical relief by
filing belated proceedings. Nor does the subsequent success of another litigant
stop or exclude the running of limitation, which begins from the date the cause
of action first arises. It is a settled principle of law that parties who fail to pursue
their remedies within the prescribed time cannot subsequently seek parity with
those who acted diligently. Therefore, the Petitioner’s reliance on the order in
GMR Warora and MSEDCL v. Adani Power is wholly misplaced. These
judgments cannot resurrect a claim that is hopelessly barred by limitation, nor
can they validate a cause of action that the Petitioner allowed to lapse through
its own prolonged and inexplicable inaction. The Petition, a textbook example
of fence-sitting, deserves dismissal on this ground alone.
(n) In any event, no Change in Law arises in the instant case, since the
Petitioner had full knowledge of and was fully aware of the Hon’ble Supreme
Court’s ongoing scrutiny and eventual cancellation of captive coal blocks,
including the Ganeshpur block; the Petitioner deliberately quoted a bid
premised on linkage coal up to 30.11.2015 and captive coal from 1.12.2015

Order in Petition No. 845/MP/2025 Page 22 of 81
